---
title: "Curtailment-to-Compute: How Much Wasted Arizona Solar Could Power Flexible AI Compute?"
author: "Working paper"
date: today
abstract: >
  Arizona's balancing authorities (APS, SRP, TEP) do not publish solar
  curtailment data, so any answer to "how much solar does Arizona waste, and
  what could flexible compute do with it?" must be estimated. We build three
  independent estimators — a per-plant-calibrated physical
  potential-vs-actual model with propagated uncertainty, a WEIM
  negative-price market signal, and documented anchors from filings and
  studies — triangulate them without ever averaging, and validate the
  machinery on a synthetic fixture with known injected curtailment before
  trusting it on real data. A flexible data-center scheduling simulation
  then translates the estimated surplus into the share of compute load it
  could serve across skeptical-to-optimistic flexibility scenarios. All
  results are ranges, not points; the data-status box on page 1 states
  exactly what the numbers in this rendering are based on.
---

## 1. The problem

Utility-scale solar is occasionally told to stop producing: *curtailed*.
CAISO publishes how much; Arizona's three large balancing authorities —
Arizona Public Service (AZPS), Salt River Project (SRP), and Tucson Electric
Power (TEPC) — do not. They report hourly demand, generation by fuel, and
interchange to EIA-930, but not curtailed MWh. Anyone claiming a number for
"wasted Arizona solar" is estimating, whether they admit it or not. We admit
it: the estimation strategy is the contribution.

The second half of the question is whether *flexible* compute — batch AI
training that can defer work into surplus hours — could productively absorb
that energy, and at what utilization cost. We simulate a configurable data
center scheduled into the estimated surplus windows and report the tradeoff
curve, under skeptical assumptions about how flexible frontier training
actually is.

## 2. Data

| Source | Role | Verification notes (live, 2026-07-07) |
|---|---|---|
| EIA-930 bulk balance CSVs | hourly BA solar + **imputation flags** | schema drift handled (2024H2 splits solar by integrated-battery status, incl. a typo in EIA's own header); physically impossible hours (>1.25× fleet AC) folded into the unusable flag |
| EIA-930 v2 API | cross-check | hourly `period` label is the hour *ending* |
| EIA-860 (2024) | fleet: location, capacity, tracking, in-service | CSP excluded (Solana); ~1.8 GW of AZ PV is in **CISO**, not the AZ BAs — modeling fleet is 89 plants / ~3.09 GW across AZPS/SRP/TEPC; phased build-outs handled per generator |
| EIA-923 monthly | per-plant calibration | primeMover='ALL' rollup rows would double-count; only 'PV' rows used |
| Open-Meteo ERA5-blend | plant-level weather (**NSRDB stand-in**) | NSRDB host not reachable from this environment; swap + sensitivity check owed |
| CAISO OASIS `PRC_INTVL_LMP` | WEIM 5-min prices, Estimator B | AZ EIM LAPs found by probing: `ELAP_{AZPS,SRP,TEPC}-APND`; data begins 2023-04; ≤7-day request spans |
| IRPs / ACC / FERC / studies | Estimator C anchors | one strong candidate logged (NREL 74176), quote verification pending |

EIA-930 unusable hours (imputed or physically impossible) are never
silently ingested: they are excluded from every sum and annual totals are
rescaled by usable-hour coverage.

## 3. Methods: three estimators, triangulated, never averaged

### 3.1 Potential model and calibration

Each plant gets a tracking-aware pvlib model (transposition, cell
temperature, PVWatts DC, inverter clipping at AC nameplate) driven by the
weather the estimator can see, scaled by the share of the plant's
generators in service each hour. Unknown per-plant parameters are fixed
assumptions absorbed by one multiplicative calibration factor per plant,
fit on presumed-unconstrained months (Jun–Sep, Dec–Jan). 30% of eligible
plant-months are held out; per-plant holdout MAE is the reported model
quality. Plants too new or too gappy in EIA-923 to calibrate get the fleet
median scale and are flagged. If the "unconstrained" months in fact contain
curtailment, Estimator A is biased **low** — the conservative direction.

### 3.2 Estimator A — potential-vs-actual gap

Curtailment proxy: calibrated potential minus reported actual, per BA-hour.
Weather error, unobserved outages, and derates are carried by the empirical
residual distribution measured on unconstrained hours; its 5th/50th/95th
percentiles generate the reported band. Clipping hourly gaps at zero turns
symmetric noise into fake positive curtailment — the validation fixture
exposed this bias directly — so A subtracts a clipped-gap false-positive
baseline measured on unconstrained hours (reported in `estimator_a_annual`,
not hidden). A sees the **union** of economic and physical curtailment plus
any residual suppression it cannot attribute.

### 3.3 Estimator B — WEIM negative-price signal

Hours with locational prices at or below zero mark market-cleared surplus:
an *economic*-curtailment signal, in hours. Converting hours to energy uses
coincident modeled potential, which yields only an **upper bound**.
Physical curtailment often produces no price signal at all, so B ≠ A by
construction, and their gap is information, not error. On real data B
covers April 2023 onward (OASIS publishes no earlier Arizona EIM LAP
prices).

### 3.4 Estimator C — documented anchors

Hand-curated statements from IRPs, ACC/FERC filings, studies, and investor
materials, each with source URL and exact quote, kept in their native units.
One strong real lead is logged as a *candidate*: NREL/CP-6A20-74176 reports
APS curtailed ≈17,100 MWh ≈ 2.9% of potential PV in 2018, entirely as
economic response to WEIM negative pricing, peaking March–April — a level,
mechanism, and seasonal shape to check our estimators against once its
quote is verified at the source (`src/estimators/c_anchors/candidates.csv`).
Unverified candidates are never loaded into figures.

### 3.5 Method validation with injected ground truth

Before trusting the estimators on Arizona, we ran the identical code on a
synthetic fixture (`src/demo_data.py`) that injects a known curtailment
schedule behind realistic obstacles: biased/noisy weather, unobserved
outages, imputed hours, measurement noise, inverter clipping. Estimator A's
5–95% band contained the injected truth in 8 of 9 BA-years (the expected
coverage of a 90% band; the miss was a heavy unobserved-outage year), with
median midpoint error ≈ 0.6 percentage points. This is an upper bound on
real-world performance — real weather error is likely worse than the
synthetic kind — but it establishes that the machinery recovers curtailment
it has never seen. Run `make demo && make test` to reproduce.

```{python}
        )
        + " (table_id: estimator_b_annual)."
    )
```

If A, B, and C disagree wildly, that finding — "Arizona has no idea how
much solar it wastes" — ships as the result. We present the range; we do
not average.

## 4. Flexible compute simulation

A data center with IT capacity, PUE, and a flexibility class (fully
deferrable / partially deferrable / firm — floors of 0%, 50%, 100% of full
load) must deliver a weekly energy SLA. A greedy scheduler serves the floor
always and places the flexible remainder into the largest surplus hours;
every contiguous flexible run pays a checkpoint/restart energy overhead; an
optional battery charges only from unabsorbed surplus. We treat *fully
deferrable* as an optimistic envelope, not a claim about frontier training —
checkpointing cost, interconnect utilization economics, and job structure
argue for the partially-deferrable rows as the realistic anchor.

## 5. Ways this could be wrong (pre-registered)

Items 1–7 were written before any real-data results existed and are kept
verbatim; item 8 was added when the weather substitution was made, before
real results were inspected.

1. **Calibration-period contamination.** If "unconstrained" months contain
   curtailment, A under-estimates. (Direction: low.)
2. **Outages and derates masquerade as curtailment.** The band carries the
   average outage rate, not outage *years*; the validation fixture produced
   exactly one such band miss in nine. (Direction: high, occasionally badly.)
3. **EIA-930 data quality.** Imputation flags now handled via the bulk
   CSVs; we additionally found and excluded physically impossible unflagged
   hours. Residual undetected reporting errors remain possible.
4. **OASIS/WEIM assumptions.** Node names and report verified live, but
   the ELAP series begins 2023-04; whether ELAP hourly means are the right
   price basis for *plant-level* economics is an assumption.
5. **Economic vs. physical.** A sees the union; B sees mostly economic. We
   report both and never allocate the difference without evidence.
6. **The compute model is stylized.** Weekly-energy SLA and a constant
   checkpoint overhead are crude proxies for real training economics;
   the fully-deferrable rows especially should be read as an envelope.
7. **Synthetic-fixture circularity risk.** The fixture's weather and fleet
   are generated by the same physical model family the estimator uses, so
   recovery results are an upper bound on real-world performance.
8. **Weather source substitution.** Plant-level irradiance is Open-Meteo
   ERA5-blend, not NSRDB. Calibration absorbs mean bias, but correlated
   weather error (e.g. monsoon cloud timing) can masquerade as curtailment
   or hide it. The NSRDB re-run is the single most important robustness
   check owed.

## 6. Replication

`make setup && make demo && make paper` reproduces the validation build
with no keys. `make real && make paper` reproduces this document's data
path (two free API keys; see SOURCES.md for the per-source verification
log). Every figure regenerates from the DuckDB store at render time; every
quantitative sentence traces to a `figure_id` or `table_id`.
